asi.hypothesis: Establish the unmodified Browse API baseline after installing the required loupe/matcher 0.4 dependency.
asi.workload: 31944 documents, 32 pages, only user-facing id retrieved
asi.environment_note: Initial checks failed because vendor had stale matcher 0.3.2 while composer.json requires ^0.4; composer update to 0.4.0 fixed unit tests and PHPStan without tracked changes.
asi.next_action_hint: Avoid decoding _document when only the configured primary key is requested; select _user_id directly while retaining internal _id ordering.

description: Avoid full document decoding for Browse ID projection

asi.hypothesis: SQLite json_extract can preserve the original scalar ID type while avoiding full _document transfer and PHP JSON decoding for primary-key-only Browse projections.
asi.learning: Direct _user_id selection would lose the distinction between integer IDs and numeric string IDs; JSON extraction preserves that API behavior.
asi.impact: Median traversal improved 41.6% and peak memory fell from 136.4 MB to 6 MB.
asi.checks: Unit tests, PHPStan, and Functional BrowseTest passed.
asi.next_action_hint: Profile the remaining 88 ms; compare json_extract against SQLite arrow syntax and investigate repeated total-hit counting or broader narrow projections.

description: Skip matches join for unconstrained Browse queries

asi.hypothesis: An empty-query, empty-filter Browse already matches the documents table, so building an all-documents CTE and joining it back to the same table is redundant.
asi.learning: Direct table scan with scalar document count preserves internal _id ordering and total-hit metadata while removing a self-join from every page.
asi.impact: Median improved 24.2% from the previous best and 55.8% from baseline; spread narrowed to 2.63 ms.
asi.checks: Unit tests, PHPStan, and Functional BrowseTest passed.
asi.next_action_hint: Measure whether scalar COUNT(*) is now repeated materially across 32 pages; test a general narrow projection or reduce OFFSET traversal cost without changing pagination semantics.

description: Compare SQLite ->> operator for primary-key extraction

asi.hypothesis: SQLite's ->> JSON scalar operator might be cheaper than json_extract for the primary-key projection.
asi.rollback_reason: Median was 2.2% slower than the 66.533500 ms best and had a wider spread; syntax-only change offered no simplification benefit.
asi.learning: Keep json_extract for this projection on the benchmark SQLite/PHP environment.
asi.next_action_hint: Target work repeated per page, especially OFFSET and result/count SQL, rather than alternate JSON syntax.

description: Read projected Browse IDs from indexed user ID

asi.hypothesis: The persisted document schema can restore the public primary-key scalar type from indexed _user_id, eliminating per-hit JSON parsing entirely.
asi.learning: TYPE_STRING can use _user_id verbatim; TYPE_NUMBER with SQLite CAST AS NUMERIC preserves integer versus real values. Other unexpected schema types retain the json_extract fallback.
asi.impact: Median improved 43.9% from the previous best and 75.2% from baseline while memory stayed at 4 MB.
asi.checks: Unit tests, PHPStan, Functional BrowseTest, and a focused integer/float/numeric-string/leading-zero-string harness passed.
asi.next_action_hint: Profile the remaining 37 ms. Test whether selecting only internal IDs then joining for the limited page reduces OFFSET work, or reduce per-page object/query construction.

description: Seek unconstrained Browse pages by internal ID

asi.hypothesis: A scalar subquery can resolve the internal-ID boundary for an offset, letting the outer ordered scan seek directly to the returned page instead of carrying OFFSET through projection.
asi.learning: Keeping resultOffset separate preserves public page metadata after resetting the SQL offset. A deleted-ID gap harness confirmed row-offset rather than numeric-ID semantics.
asi.impact: Median improved 7.3% from the previous best and 77.0% from baseline.
asi.checks: Unit tests, PHPStan, Functional BrowseTest, and deleted-ID offset/page harness passed.
asi.next_action_hint: The gain is smaller and run spread is wider; confirm once, then inspect per-page PHP construction or scalar count overhead.

asi.hypothesis: A second run should remain materially below the 37.354167 ms prior best if the seek improvement is real.
asi.rollback_reason: The confirmation was slower than experiment 6, so it does not replace the recorded best; no uncommitted production changes existed to revert.
asi.learning: The confirmed median remains 5.0% below the pre-seek best, supporting the committed change despite ordinary run-to-run noise.
asi.next_action_hint: Optimize a structurally different repeated cost rather than micro-tuning the seek SQL.

description: Count unconstrained Browse hits outside result rows

asi.hypothesis: Fetching totalHits independently avoids materializing and transferring the same scalar count in every one of 31944 result rows.
asi.learning: One cheap count query per request costs less than an extra totalHits column on every hit. The independent count also remains available when an offset returns no rows.
asi.impact: Median improved 7.6% from the best committed seek run and 78.7% from baseline.
asi.checks: Unit tests, PHPStan, and Functional BrowseTest passed.
asi.next_action_hint: Try bypassing unused empty-query Searcher pipeline setup, but reject a large duplicated fast path unless the gain is material.

description: Add direct path for browsing primary keys

asi.hypothesis: The dominant remaining overhead is constructing and running the general Searcher pipeline 32 times for a workload requiring only ordered primary keys.
asi.learning: A narrow Engine fast path can reuse all established SQL semantics while avoiding parser, filter builder, sorting, token, CTE, and result hydration setup. Query/filter or broader projections still fall back to Searcher.
asi.impact: Median improved 29.2% from the prior best and 84.9% from baseline; spread narrowed to 1.74 ms.
asi.checks: Unit tests, PHPStan, BrowseTest, custom-primary-key and queried-fallback cases, typed IDs, and deleted-ID pagination passed.
asi.next_action_hint: Profile the 22.7 ms floor. Avoid duplicating more logic for tiny gains; consider query-builder/result iteration overhead or document-count caching only if concurrency semantics stay correct.

description: Stream direct primary-key SQL without QueryBuilder

asi.hypothesis: Avoiding QueryBuilder construction and streaming Result::iterateColumn might reduce per-page setup and temporary arrays.
asi.rollback_reason: Median regressed 6.2% from 22.650583 ms and spread widened; fetchFirstColumn materialization is faster for 1000-value pages.
asi.learning: DBAL QueryBuilder overhead is smaller than generator iteration overhead in this workload. Keep the materialized fetchFirstColumn path.
asi.next_action_hint: Do not pursue streaming for small bounded pages. Investigate count-query cost or stop before added complexity outweighs gains.

asi.hypothesis: Rerunning the unchanged best implementation should confirm that the dedicated Engine path remains decisively faster after the discarded streaming experiment.
asi.learning: The direct path repeated below its initial measurement with lower spread; QueryBuilder fetchFirstColumn remains the correct local optimum.
asi.impact: Confirmed median is 86.9% below baseline with peak memory reduced from 136.4 MB to 4 MB.
asi.checks: Unit tests and PHPStan passed on unchanged production code.
asi.next_action_hint: Current implementation is near the measured direct-DBAL floor. Shift to a structurally different idea only; avoid micro-optimizations within normal noise.

asi.hypothesis: A read transaction can preserve the old single-statement snapshot semantics after splitting totalHits from page rows, with negligible cost.
asi.learning: The transaction adds about 0.6 ms versus the unusually fast prior rerun and remains faster than the direct path's initial measurement. Fast-path placement inside the reindex catch and fallback for invalid pagination are required correctness guards.
asi.impact: Correctness-hardened implementation remains 86.5% faster than baseline and uses 4 MB peak memory.
asi.checks: Unit tests, PHPStan, BrowseTest, and negative-offset legacy behavior passed.
asi.next_action_hint: Current path is at the direct DBAL floor. Prefer reviewing robustness and reducing duplication over speculative micro-optimization.

name: Browse API projection via SQLite json_extract

description: Baseline: browse projections always select and JSON-decode the full _document

asi.hypothesis: Establish a baseline for four browse projection workloads on the 31944-document movies corpus.
asi.workload: 32 pages x 1000 docs, four projections: primary key only, 3-attribute subset, whole document, filtered subset
asi.current_implementation: Searcher::selectDocuments() always adds documents._document; fetchResult() calls Util::decodeJson() per hit then array_intersect_key().
asi.environment_note: phpunit needed memory_limit=1G in .auto/checks.sh; the 128M default OOMs in vendor/toflar/fast-set unrelated to this work.
asi.next_action_hint: Project only requested attributes with SQLite json_extract instead of transferring/decoding the whole document; add a direct path when only the primary key is asked for.

name: Browse API projection via SQLite json_extract (6 workloads incl. large documents)

description: Baseline on six browse workloads including a 4 KB-document corpus

asi.hypothesis: The 510-byte movies corpus hides the value of a narrow projection; add a 20000-document/4 KB-body corpus so the benchmark reflects page/article indexing before changing src.
asi.probe_size_scaling: Standalone PDO probe: json_extract multipath vs full-document decode is -2% at 500 B docs, -37% at 2 KB, -73% at 10 KB. Primary-key-only via _user_id is -75% to -96% at every size.
asi.probe_sql_variants: On the movies DB (510 B docs, 32 pages): full decode 124.2 ms, json_extract multipath 101.5 ms, json_object+json_extract 119.4 ms, per-attribute -> columns 124.6 ms, json_group_object over json_each 139.3 ms, _user_id only 51.9 ms.
asi.open_semantics_questions: Multipath json_extract returns values in requested (sorted) order rather than document order, and cannot distinguish an absent key from a JSON null. Both are observable through assertSame in the functional tests.
asi.next_action_hint: Implement Searcher projection via json_extract plus an Engine primary-key-only path, then measure which functional tests fail on key order.

description: Answer primary-key-only browsing straight from the documents table with json_extract

asi.hypothesis: An unfiltered, unqueried browse that asks only for the primary key needs neither the document body nor the Searcher pipeline; json_extract on the stored document returns the id with its original scalar type.
asi.impact: pk_ms 137.89 -> 45.68 ms (-67%); total 1749.39 -> 1687.17 ms. Other five workloads unchanged within noise.
asi.why_json_extract_over_user_id: _user_id is a TEXT column, so an integer id would come back as a string. json_extract preserves the stored JSON type exactly, which a differential harness confirmed for integer, float, leading-zero-string and digit-only-string primary keys.
asi.checks: Unit + functional suites, PHPStan, plus a differential harness comparing the fast path to the Searcher path over offset/limit/page pagination, deleted-id gaps, and filter fallback.
asi.pre_existing_finding: A float primary key of 3.0 already comes back as int 3 on both paths because Util::encodeJson drops the zero fraction. Not a regression.
asi.next_action_hint: The generic subset projection is still open: plain multipath json_extract breaks 62 tests because it reorders hit keys and cannot tell an absent attribute from a null one.

description: Project subsets with json_group_object over json_each (exact but slower overall)

asi.hypothesis: json_group_object over json_each with a CASE that restores JSON types is the only single-parse projection that keeps document key order and tells an absent attribute from a null one, so it should be adoptable without touching a single test.
asi.correctness_result: All 378 unit + functional tests passed unchanged, confirming the formulation is byte-identical to decoding the whole document.
asi.rollback_reason: Total regressed 1687.17 -> 1716.03 ms. It won on 4 KB documents (large_subset 568.86 -> 528.29) but lost badly on the 510-byte movies corpus (subset 126.90 -> 179.89, +42%) because json_each pays virtual-table overhead per document key regardless of document size.
asi.key_finding: large_subset is 568 ms while a raw PDO loop over the same 20 pages of 4 KB documents takes only ~138 ms, so roughly 75% of browse time is Searcher pipeline construction, not document decoding. Projection can only ever address the remaining quarter.
asi.next_action_hint: Generalise the direct browse path from primary-key-only to any unqueried, unfiltered browse so the whole Searcher pipeline is skipped; do the projection there where no CTE overhead masks it.

description: Answer every unqueried, unfiltered browse straight from the documents table

asi.hypothesis: A browse without a query and without a filter matches every document, so the CTE pipeline, filter builder, tokenizer and sorting setup are pure overhead; the documents table alone answers it in the same internal id order.
asi.surprise: The 4 KB-document workloads did not move at all (large_subset 568.86 -> 573.98, large_whole 581.90 -> 575.82), so the previous run's inference that 75% of browse time is pipeline construction only holds for small documents. On large documents the cost is document transfer and decoding.
asi.checks: Unit + functional suites, PHPStan, plus a 73-comparison differential harness that runs every projection through both the direct path and the Searcher path (forced with an always-true filter) and compares toArray() and json_encode of the hits, covering nested objects, booleans, floats, explicit nulls, absent attributes and unknown attributes.
asi.next_action_hint: Profile the 574 ms of large_subset: a raw PDO loop over the same pages costs ~138 ms, so find whether the gap is DBAL row fetching, JSON decoding or SQLite reads before trying a projection again.
